subsection: 13. Church-state relations under Mussolini and Hitler; Anglo-American popular culture: radio and cinema

notes.h: Background: the Roman Question and Mussolini's dictatorship
notes.b: Church-state relations in Italy began with a quarrel that was almost sixty years old. Mussolini inherited it and chose to settle it rather than fight the Church.
points: In 1870 Italian troops took Rome and ended the Papal States (the lands the popes had ruled as kings). The popes refused to recognise the Kingdom of Italy and called themselves "prisoners in the Vatican". This dispute is known as the Roman Question.
For decades Catholics were told not to take part in national politics, so the quarrel kept many devout Italians at a distance from the state that ruled them.

Mussolini became Prime Minister in October 1922 and by 1926 ruled a one-party state, a dictatorship in which only the Fascist Party was allowed, so the Church had to deal with one ruler rather than many parties.
Fascism began anticlerical (hostile to the Church), but Mussolini dropped this stance because he needed the support of Catholics and conservatives to hold power.

The Vatican let the Catholic Popular Party (the Partito Popolare, or Popolari) go, so the Church no longer had a party of its own in politics. Its leader, the priest Luigi Sturzo, resigned in 1923 and went into exile in 1924.

notes.h: Why Mussolini and Pius XI wanted a deal
notes.b: By the late 1920s each side had something the other could give. Neither was acting out of friendship: both were pursuing their own interests.
points: Mussolini wanted the support of a Catholic nation, because the Church's approval would give his regime legitimacy (acceptance as the rightful government) at home and prestige abroad.
Pope Pius XI (pope from February 1922 until his death in February 1939) wanted the Roman Question settled, so that the Church's position in Italy rested on a firm legal footing.

He also wanted Catholic life protected, including Church schools, Catholic marriage and Catholic Action (the Church's organisation for lay people, meaning ordinary Catholics who are not clergy), and he saw Mussolini as an ally against communism.
notes.tip: Examiners like cause and result: Mussolini's need for Catholic support led to the Lateran Treaties, which brought Catholic backing and a lasting settlement. Ordinary Level questions often ask why each side signed.

notes.h: The Lateran Treaties, 11 February 1929: the terms
notes.b: The Lateran Treaties were the great settlement between the Italian state and the papacy. They were three agreements in one, each dealing with a different part of the quarrel.
points: They were signed at the Lateran Palace in Rome on 11 February 1929 by Mussolini and Cardinal Pietro Gasparri, the Vatican Secretary of State (the pope's chief minister), and were ratified (formally approved) in June 1929.

The three documents were a treaty (creating Vatican City), a financial convention (dealing with compensation) and a concordat (an agreement between the pope and a state about the Church's place in that country).
The treaty made Vatican City an independent sovereign state of about 44 hectares, so the pope ruled his own territory. In return the papacy recognised the Kingdom of Italy with Rome as its capital.
The financial convention gave the Church compensation of 1.75 billion lire (750 million in cash and 1 billion in state bonds) for the Papal States lost in 1870.

Under the concordat, Catholicism became the sole religion of the state, and religious teaching was provided in state primary and secondary schools, which gave the Church a say in how the young were taught.
Church marriage became valid in civil law, so couples married in church were legally married. Bishops had to swear loyalty to the state.
Catholic Action was allowed to continue, but only if it stayed out of politics. This condition shows that the Church's gains came with strings attached.
notes.tip: Give the exact date, both signatories and the terms in order: Vatican City, compensation, Catholicism as state religion, religious teaching, marriage. Do not mix this up with the Reich Concordat of 1933: only the Lateran Treaties created Vatican City.

notes.h: Results of the Lateran Treaties for Mussolini
notes.b: The settlement paid off for Mussolini almost at once, and it proved more lasting than his regime.
points: In the plebiscite election of March 1929 voters were offered a single list of Fascist candidates and approved it by an overwhelming majority, with Catholic organisations urging a yes vote. This showed what Church backing was worth to him.
Mussolini gained the support of the Catholic majority, and the Church's endorsement helped legitimise the regime in the eyes of many Italians.
He also won prestige abroad. Pius XI publicly praised him, describing him as a man sent by Providence (God's guiding care).
The settlement is often called Mussolini's most lasting achievement. It outlived Fascism, and the concordat was revised only in 1984, when Catholicism ceased to be the state religion of Italy.

notes.h: The Catholic Action dispute, 1931
notes.b: The partnership soon met its first limit. A dictatorship wants to shape the young, and the Church had its own organisations for doing exactly that.
points: Catholic Action's youth and student groups worried the regime, because the Fascists saw them as rivals to the Fascist youth movement.
Fascist squads attacked Catholic centres, and the regime dissolved the Catholic youth organisations in May 1931, because it would not tolerate a rival for the loyalty of the young.

Pius XI replied with the encyclical (a formal letter from the pope to the whole Church) Non abbiamo bisogno (We have no need), issued in Italian on 29 June 1931. It condemned the regime's claim to monopolise the young.

The dispute ended in a compromise agreement in September 1931. Catholic Action survived under the bishops, but it was confined to religious, cultural and charitable activities, and its youth groups were kept out of politics and sport.
Apart from this encyclical, the Church's objections were mostly made in private diplomacy and in the Vatican's press, and Pius XI rarely challenged Mussolini openly.
notes.tip: Use the chain: the Fascist claim to a youth monopoly led to the 1931 clash, which ended in compromise. Keep Non abbiamo bisogno (1931, Italy, in Italian) apart from Mit brennender Sorge (1937, Germany, in German).

notes.h: The racial laws, 1938
notes.b: Italy's alliance with Nazi Germany pulled the regime towards racial policy. This tested the Church's relationship with the regime a second time.
points: Following the Axis (the alliance between Italy and Germany), Mussolini's regime published the Manifesto of the Race on 14 July 1938, which defined the racial basis of Italian identity.

Racial laws followed between September and November 1938, in line with Germany's policy. They excluded Jews from state schools, the professions and the armed forces, and banned marriage between Italians and Jews.
Pius XI objected above all to the marriage ban, which also covered Jews who had become Catholics, because he saw it as a breach of the marriage terms of the concordat.
In September 1938 he told Belgian pilgrims, "Spiritually, we are Semites." The remark stressed the link between Christians and Jews, but it was a spoken comment, not a break with the regime.
The Church protested but did not break with the regime.
Pius XI died in February 1939. His successor, Pius XII (Eugenio Pacelli, elected in March 1939), was more cautious.
notes.tip: Say that the Church protested, mainly over the marriage ban, but did not break with the regime. Writing that it withdrew its support over the racial laws is wrong.

notes.h: Background: Germany and the churches in 1933
notes.b: Hitler faced a different religious map from Mussolini's. Germany was split between two large churches, and both had reasons to be wary of a Nazi government.
points: Germany was about two-thirds Protestant and one-third Catholic. The Protestants were divided into 28 regional (Land) churches, so there was no single Protestant Church for Hitler to deal with.
Catholics remembered the Kulturkampf, Bismarck's struggle with the Catholic Church in the 1870s, and so they knew what it was to have the state turn against them.

Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933. The Enabling Act (23 March 1933, which let him make laws without parliament) passed with the votes of the Catholic Centre Party, and Gleichschaltung began, the bringing of every organisation into line with Nazi control.
The Nazi Party programme of 1920 promised "positive Christianity". Hitler courted the churches in 1933 while planning to subordinate them (bring them under Nazi control).

Leading Nazis such as Alfred Rosenberg, Martin Bormann and Himmler were hostile to Christianity. Rosenberg's The Myth of the Twentieth Century (1930) was placed on the Church's Index of forbidden books in 1934.
The German bishops lifted their ban on Catholics joining the Nazi Party on 28 March 1933, which removed one barrier between Catholics and the new regime.
notes.tip: Keep three groups apart: the German Christians (pro-Nazi Protestants), the Confessing Church (Protestant opposition) and the Catholic Church (covered by the Concordat). The Reichskirche concerned Protestants only.

notes.h: The Reich Concordat, July 1933
notes.b: Within months of taking power Hitler offered the Catholic Church the kind of agreement Mussolini had made. For him it was a way to win respectability while ending Catholic politics.
points: The Reich Concordat was signed in Rome on 20 July 1933 by Cardinal Eugenio Pacelli (the Vatican Secretary of State, later Pius XII) and Vice-Chancellor Franz von Papen.
The Church kept freedom of worship, its schools, religious teaching and its religious organisations. In return clergy were barred from party politics and bishops swore loyalty to the state.
The Centre Party, the main Catholic party, dissolved itself on 5 July 1933, as the Concordat was being concluded, so Catholic organisations in Germany lost much of their political role.
Hitler's gains were international respectability, because a treaty with the Vatican made his regime look acceptable abroad, and the end of political Catholicism.
notes.tip: Date the Reich Concordat exactly, 20 July 1933. Both dictators began with a concordat, and that parallel is the start of a good comparative answer.

notes.h: Breaking the Concordat, 1934-1937
notes.b: The Concordat did not protect the Church for long. The regime wanted total loyalty, so it squeezed Catholic organisations and then persecuted the clergy.
points: On 30 June 1934, in the Night of the Long Knives, Erich Klausener, head of Catholic Action in Berlin, was murdered, a warning that Catholic leaders were not safe.
Catholic youth groups were squeezed and then banned as the Hitler Youth became compulsory (the Hitler Youth law was passed in December 1936), because the regime wanted to claim the young for itself.
By the end of the 1930s Catholic schools had been replaced by state community schools, and the Catholic press was curbed.
In 1936-37 the regime staged morality trials of priests and members of religious orders, show trials meant to blacken the clergy's reputation.
Clergy were sent to camps, such as Dachau, where there was a priests' block.
Popular protest could win locally: the order removing crucifixes from schools in Oldenburg was withdrawn after protests in 1936.
In short, the Nazi regime violated the Concordat within a few years, closing Catholic schools and youth organisations and arresting priests and members of religious orders.
notes.tip: Use the chain: the Concordat led to the end of the Centre Party, the Concordat was then broken, and Pius XI answered with Mit brennender Sorge.

notes.h: The Reichskirche and the German Christians
notes.b: The Reichskirche (Reich Church) was Hitler's plan for the Protestants. With 28 regional churches, one Church under Nazi control looked like an easy way to bring all Protestants into line.
points: The Reichskirche was to be a single, centralised Protestant Church loyal to the Nazi state. It would replace the 28 regional churches and end their independence.
Its backers were the German Christians (Deutsche Christen), a pro-Nazi movement within Protestantism founded in 1932, who wanted a Christianity fitted to Nazi ideas.
Two of their demands were the Aryan paragraph, which barred pastors of Jewish descent so that Jewish Christians were excluded from church office, and talk of dropping the Old Testament.
The German Christians won about two-thirds of the votes in the Protestant church elections of July 1933, which gave them control of the church machinery.
Ludwig Müller, Hitler's adviser on church affairs, became Reich Bishop in September 1933, but his leadership was challenged within the churches.
notes.tip: The German Christians wanted a Christianity reshaped by Nazi racial ideas, not abolished, so do not write that they planned to do away with Christian doctrine. Ludwig Müller (Reich Bishop), Martin Niemöller (Confessing Church) and Hanns Kerrl (Minister for Church Affairs) are easily confused.

notes.h: Why the Reichskirche failed
notes.b: The Reichskirche failed. Its own extremism drove moderate Protestants away, and the regime could not bring the churches to heel even when it tried direct control.
points: A mass German Christian rally in Berlin's Sportpalast in November 1933, demanding that the Old Testament be dropped, drove moderates away.
Müller never controlled the churches and was sidelined, because most Protestants would not accept a Reich Bishop imposed by the state.
In 1935 the regime set up a Ministry for Church Affairs under Hanns Kerrl to impose control directly, with little more success.
The Protestant churches split three ways: the German Christians, the Confessing Church, and a cautious neutral majority.
notes.tip: Use the chain: the drive for a Reichskirche led to Barmen and the Confessing Church, and then to the failure of the Reichskirche.

notes.h: The Confessing Church and the Barmen Declaration
notes.b: Protestants who refused the Reich Church formed their own opposition. It was about defending the Church's independence, not about overthrowing Hitler.
points: The Confessing Church grew from Martin Niemöller's Pastors' Emergency League, formed in September 1933 with several thousand pastors.
The Barmen Declaration of 31 May 1934, mainly drafted by the Swiss theologian Karl Barth, said that the Church answered to Christ, not to the state or a Führer (the Nazi leader).
It defended the Church's independence and its teaching, and so rejected the state's claim to control what the Church taught.
It did not set out to overthrow the regime, and few of its members spoke up for Jews who were not Christians.

notes.h: Two Protestant opponents: Niemöller and Bonhoeffer
notes.b: Two men came to stand for Protestant resistance. Their fates were very different, and examiners expect you to keep them apart.
points: Martin Niemöller was a U-boat commander in the First World War and then a pastor at Dahlem in Berlin. He at first welcomed the Nazis, but he founded the Pastors' Emergency League and led the Confessing Church.
He was arrested on 1 July 1937 and tried in 1938. He was held in Sachsenhausen and then Dachau concentration camps as Hitler's personal prisoner until 1945, so he survived the war.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, born in 1906, was a Lutheran theologian of the Confessing Church. From 1935 he ran its secret seminary at Finkenwalde, which the Gestapo (the Nazi secret state police) closed in 1937.
He moved from church opposition to active resistance through contacts in military intelligence (the Abwehr) and the plotters against Hitler, and he was arrested in April 1943.
Bonhoeffer was executed at Flossenbürg concentration camp on 9 April 1945.
notes.tip: Barmen, Niemöller and Bonhoeffer are the named evidence for Protestant opposition. Remember that Niemöller survived the camps while Bonhoeffer was executed in April 1945.

notes.h: Catholic protest: Mit brennender Sorge and Galen
notes.b: Catholic opposition came from the top of the Church, through the pope's encyclical and the sermons of one bishop. Both defended Catholic institutions and teaching against Nazi persecution.
points: Mit brennender Sorge (With burning concern), dated 14 March 1937, was an encyclical by Pius XI written in German. Cardinal Michael von Faulhaber, Archbishop of Munich, and Pacelli helped draft it.
It condemned breaches of the Concordat and the worship of race and state, so it attacked both the regime's broken promises and its ideology.
It was smuggled into Germany and read from Catholic pulpits on Palm Sunday, 21 March 1937. The Gestapo seized copies and closed the printers, and the persecution of the clergy increased.

Clemens August von Galen, Bishop of Münster from 1933 and nicknamed the Lion of Münster, attacked Gestapo seizures of church property in sermons in July and August 1941. He also attacked the killing of disabled people in the T4 euthanasia programme.
The T4 programme was officially halted in August 1941, but the killings continued in secret.
The regime did not arrest Galen, for fear of Catholic opinion in wartime.
notes.tip: Name both encyclicals with their year and country. Do not write that Galen simply stopped the T4 programme: it was officially halted and killing went on in secret. Galen (Münster, 1941 sermons) is not Faulhaber (Munich, 1937 encyclical).

notes.h: The limits of church opposition
notes.b: Church protest was real but narrow. The churches mostly defended themselves, and historians still argue about how far that was a moral failure.
points: The churches defended their own institutions and teaching far more than the victims of the regime. Their protests were limited to defending themselves and to opposing the euthanasia programme.
There was little public protest at the persecution of the Jews. Kristallnacht (9-10 November 1938) passed without an official protest from either church.
Most clergy and churchgoers conformed, for example by staying silent, and many backed the war.

Pius XII's Christmas broadcast of 1942 spoke of people killed because of their nationality or race, without naming the Jews or Germany. Critics such as John Cornwell (Hitler's Pope, 1999) call this silence complicity.
Defenders of Pius XII say that public protest would have made things worse, and they point to Catholic help for Jews in hiding.

Bormann, Himmler and Rosenberg intended to destroy the churches' influence after the war. The German Faith Movement and neo-pagan ideas (a revival of pre-Christian religion) had little popular following.
notes.tip: A closing paragraph on the Pius XII debate or the limits of church protest earns evaluation marks. Give both sides, and keep Pius XI (Lateran Treaties, both encyclicals) apart from Pius XII (the Reich Concordat negotiator and the wartime silence debate).

notes.h: Comparing the two dictators and the churches
notes.b: Put side by side, the two stories follow one pattern. The difference lies in how much each dictator needed the Church.
points: Both dictators began with a concordat, in 1929 and in 1933, and both later clashed with the Church over youth and race.
Mussolini needed the Church and kept a working partnership, so his clashes ended in compromise in 1931 and in protest without a break in 1938.
Hitler saw the churches as rivals for total loyalty, so he moved from courtship to persecution.
The churches survived both regimes as the largest institutions outside party control.
notes.tip: Higher Level marks go to a comparative thesis argued throughout, not two separate narratives. A strong line is that both began with an agreement and moved to conflict, but Mussolini kept a working partnership while Hitler moved to persecution.

notes.h: Radio: the BBC and Reith
notes.b: From the early 1920s radio brought news, music, sport, comedy and the voices of leaders into the home. Governments quickly saw that it could inform, entertain and persuade all at once.
points: Cheap sets made radio affordable, so Britain had about 9 million radio licences by 1939.
The British Broadcasting Company was founded in 1922, with John Reith as its general manager.
On 1 January 1927 it became the British Broadcasting Corporation under a royal charter (a formal grant from the Crown), with Reith as its first director-general until 1938.
The BBC was a monopoly funded by the licence fee that listeners paid, with no advertising, so it did not depend on advertisers.
Reith's public-service ideal, broadcasting for the public good rather than profit, was to "inform, educate and entertain", and Sunday programming was strict.
The Empire Service began in 1932, so that BBC programmes reached listeners across the British Empire.
notes.tip: Say that the BBC became a corporation in 1927 under Reith. In 1922 it was a company and Reith was only its general manager; he became the first director-general in 1927.

notes.h: Commercial radio: American networks and Radio Luxembourg
notes.b: The American model was the opposite of the BBC's. Radio there was paid for by advertisers, and it challenged British ideas of what radio should be.
points: NBC (founded 1926) and CBS (founded 1927) were American networks, meaning chains of stations broadcasting the same programmes. They were commercial, paid for by advertisers, who sponsored whole programmes.
Programmes included comedy, variety, dance bands and serials, which were nicknamed soap operas after their soap-company sponsors.
Radio Luxembourg began English-language programmes in 1933, beamed into Britain, especially on Sundays. It played the dance music and American-style shows that the BBC avoided.
It was the most famous commercial challenger to the BBC monopoly, alongside Radio Normandy, which had been broadcasting English-language commercial programmes to Britain since 1931.
notes.tip: Contrasting the BBC's public-service model with American commercial radio is an exam point. Do not call Radio Luxembourg the first challenger to the BBC: Radio Normandy came earlier.

notes.h: Radio and politics: fireside chats and The War of the Worlds
notes.b: Radio changed how leaders spoke to their people. In a democracy it allowed explanation and reassurance, and it also showed how tightly a broadcast could grip an audience.
points: President Franklin Roosevelt gave his first fireside chat, a radio talk in a relaxed, conversational style, on 12 March 1933, during the banking crisis.
About 30 fireside chats followed, up to 1944, so Roosevelt could speak directly to listeners about the New Deal and later the war.
A democratic leader explaining and reassuring by radio contrasts with the dictators' mass rallies.
Orson Welles directed and starred in The War of the Worlds, a drama about a Martian invasion, broadcast by CBS on 30 October 1938.
Newspaper reports of mass panic were exaggerated, but the broadcast showed radio's hold on listeners.
notes.tip: Fireside chats are named evidence of the democratic use of radio, so give the first date, 12 March 1933. Pair them with BBC news and Chaplin's satire when you argue democratic use against dictatorial control.

notes.h: Radio in wartime Britain
notes.b: In the Second World War the BBC became a tool of morale, information and resistance, and its reputation for truth was one of its great assets.
points: The BBC Home Service began in September 1939, and the Forces Programme, lighter in tone for the troops, began in January 1940.
BBC news bulletins were trusted at home and in occupied Europe, and gained a reputation for trustworthy reporting in contrast to German propaganda.
Churchill made radio broadcasts to the nation at key moments, so the whole country could hear its leader at once.
De Gaulle made a broadcast appeal to the French on the BBC on 18 June 1940, which shows how radio could reach people across a occupied frontier.
The V for Victory campaign of 1941 was run over the BBC, and broadcasts to occupied Europe included coded messages to resistance groups.
ITMA (It's That Man Again), a BBC comedy with Tommy Handley from 1939, helped to keep up spirits.
notes.tip: Use named programmes and dates rather than talk of the media in general: the Home Service, the Forces Programme, de Gaulle's appeal, V for Victory and ITMA make a wartime radio paragraph concrete.

notes.h: Radio in wartime: American voices and the enemy's
notes.b: Radio was heard across the front lines. American broadcasters built sympathy for Britain, while Germany's radio used propaganda and, by accident, a song that both sides loved.
points: Edward R. Murrow broadcast for CBS from London during the Blitz in 1940-41, opening with "This is London", and his reports built American sympathy for Britain.
The American Forces Network began broadcasting in Britain on 4 July 1943. It played American music and gave news to troops and, unofficially, to British listeners.
Glenn Miller's American band broadcast to the forces. Miller disappeared over the English Channel in December 1944.
William Joyce, known as Lord Haw-Haw, broadcast Nazi propaganda from Germany to Britain from 1939. He was more mocked than believed, and he was hanged for treason in January 1946.
Lili Marleen, in Lale Andersen's recording of 1939, was broadcast nightly from the German forces' radio station in Belgrade from 1941. It was loved by soldiers on both sides in North Africa.
notes.tip: Keep Lord Haw-Haw (Nazi radio to Britain) apart from Murrow (American radio from Britain). The Home Service and Forces Programme are BBC, the American Forces Network is the US military, and it began in 1943, not 1942.

notes.h: Cinema: mass entertainment and the talkies
notes.b: In the 1920s and 1930s going to the pictures became the most popular entertainment of the age. Then sound changed the industry almost overnight.
points: By the late 1930s Britain had about 20 million cinema admissions a week, many in large cinemas called picture palaces.
Audiences were strongly young, female and working-class, and going to the pictures was a weekly habit because tickets were cheap and cinemas were everywhere.

The Jazz Singer (Warner Bros, 1927), starring Al Jolson, was the first feature film with synchronised singing and speech. It was not entirely spoken, but it began the talkies and led to their rapid spread.
By the early 1930s silent films were finished.
The effects of sound included new stars and musicals, language barriers in Europe that were met with dubbing and subtitles, and the strength of English-language films in Britain.
notes.tip: Use the chain: the talkies of 1927 led to the end of silent film and an English-language advantage for Hollywood, which led to European quotas and protection. The Jazz Singer began the talkies but was not entirely spoken.

notes.h: The Hollywood studio system
notes.b: Hollywood's world dominance came from the way the film business was organised, not only from the films themselves.
points: A few major studios (MGM, Paramount, Warner Bros, 20th Century Fox and RKO) controlled production, distribution and many cinemas. This is called vertical integration, meaning that one company owns every stage from making a film to showing it, so the studios could make sure their films got screens.
Stars were tied to the studios by long contracts, so the studios controlled their careers.
Genres included musicals, gangster films, westerns and comedies, as well as cartoons such as Disney's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937).
The Production Code, known as the Hays Code, was adopted in 1930 and strictly enforced from 1934. It governed morality on screen, so studios cut scenes to avoid banned content.
The studios produced and distributed most of the films shown in Britain and Europe, so Hollywood dominated the world market.

notes.h: Hollywood in Europe and the British response
notes.b: American films filled most of the screen time in Britain, so Britain acted to protect its own industry and still produced some films of its own that succeeded.
points: By the late 1930s Hollywood films filled most screens in Britain and much of Europe.
The Cinematograph Films Act (1927) required distributors and cinemas to show a quota of British films, which rose over ten years, to protect the domestic industry from American competition.
The quota produced many cheap quota quickies, but it also protected a home industry.
British films that succeeded included Alexander Korda's The Private Life of Henry VIII (1933), a success in America, and Alfred Hitchcock's The 39 Steps (1935).
Gracie Fields and George Formby were popular British comedians.
notes.tip: Hollywood's appeal against fears of Americanisation is a paired point that examiners reward. The Act and the quota are your evidence of how Britain protected its own industry.

notes.h: Newsreels
notes.b: For many people in the 1930s the only moving pictures of real events came from the newsreels shown in cinemas.
points: Newsreels were short news films shown before the main feature, so a whole cinema audience saw the same pictures of events.
The main British newsreels were British Pathé and British Movietone News (from 1929). The American newsreel The March of Time began in 1935.
They were generally patriotic and deferential (respectful towards those in authority), so they supported rather than questioned governments.
Germany and Italy used newsreels for propaganda, while the Hollywood and British newsreels worked within a free press.
notes.tip: Keep newsreels (short news films in cinemas), documentaries (Jennings, Capra) and feature films apart. Examiners reward named examples, not general claims about the media.

notes.h: Wartime films in Britain and America
notes.b: In wartime governments and studios used film to lift morale and to explain what the fighting was for.
points: Humphrey Jennings made the documentaries Listen to Britain (1942) and Fires Were Started (1943).
Noël Coward's naval drama In Which We Serve (1942) was a wartime morale film. It was a private production made with the Navy's help.
Laurence Olivier's Henry V (1944) was patriotic spectacle, and British films stressed a people's war of all classes.
In America, Mrs Miniver (1942) pictured an English family in the war. It won the Oscar for Best Picture and built support for Britain.
Casablanca (1942) was another Hollywood film of the war years.
Frank Capra's Why We Fight series (1942-45) explained the war to American servicemen, and the American government used films to explain the war to the public.

notes.h: The dictatorships and American film
notes.b: The dictatorships distrusted Hollywood's hold over their audiences, so they built or protected their own industries, though their cinema-goers still loved American films.
points: Fascist Italy built the Cinecittà studios, opened by Mussolini in 1937, and began the Venice Film Festival in 1932.
From 1938 the Italian state held a monopoly on importing foreign films, after which the major American studios withdrew from Italy.
Nazi Germany censored and restricted American films in the 1930s and banned them in the war. German cinema came to be dominated by home-made films and newsreels.
Hollywood stayed popular with audiences in both countries, which is why the regimes kept needing restrictions.
Both regimes also ran their own propaganda machines, Goebbels's ministry in Germany and Mussolini's Istituto Luce in Italy, which offer a contrast with Anglo-American radio and cinema.
notes.tip: Give the 1938 import monopoly as Italy's main measure against Hollywood. For Germany, say American films were restricted in the 1930s and banned in the war.

notes.h: Key personality: Charlie Chaplin
notes.b: Chaplin was a British-born comedian and film-maker whose Tramp character made him the most famous film star of the silent era, and whose later films criticised modern society and the dictators. He shaped popular culture rather than simply witnessing it.
points: Chaplin was born in London on 16 April 1889 (four days before Hitler), into poverty, and began as a child performer in the music hall. He toured the USA with Fred Karno's comedy company from 1910 and joined Mack Sennett's Keystone studio in late 1913.

The Tramp first appeared in 1914: a little man with bowler hat, cane and baggy trousers, poor but dignified. He was developed in The Kid (1921), The Gold Rush (1925) and City Lights (1931, still silent, with a music score).

In 1919 Chaplin co-founded United Artists with Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks and D.W. Griffith, so he owned his films and worked independently of the major studios. He resisted talkies longer than anyone.

Modern Times (1936) showed the Tramp as a factory worker caught in the machine, in a world of unemployment and the Depression. It gave social comment through comedy, and it was the first film in which his voice was heard, in a nonsense song, and the Tramp's last appearance.

The Great Dictator (1940) was his first full talking picture. He played two parts: Adenoid Hynkel, dictator of Tomania and a parody of Hitler, and a Jewish barber who is mistaken for him. Benzino Napaloni of Bacteria parodied Mussolini.

The film ends with the barber's speech for peace and humanity. Made while the USA was still neutral, it was his biggest box-office success and won five Academy Award nominations. In his 1964 autobiography he said he could not have made it had he known the truth of the camps.

Contemporaries saw him as the world's most famous film star, loved across Europe, though the Nazis banned his films. In the United States he was attacked for his left-wing views and private life, and in 1952, while he was travelling to London, his permission to re-enter the USA was withdrawn.

He settled in Switzerland, received an honorary Oscar in 1972 and a knighthood in 1975, and died in 1977. Historians see him as a founder of film comedy as an art and proof that cinema could carry political criticism; they debate his later films' politics.
notes.tip: Keep Modern Times (1936, industrial society) apart from The Great Dictator (1940, Hitler). In the second film Hynkel is the Hitler parody and the barber is a separate character, both played by Chaplin. Do not say he belonged to the studio system.

notes.h: Key personality: Bing Crosby
notes.b: Crosby was an American singer and actor whose radio shows, records and films made him the most popular entertainer of his age, and whose songs were heard across the world during the war.
points: Crosby was born in Tacoma, Washington, on 3 May 1903. In the late 1920s he sang with Paul Whiteman's band as one of the Rhythm Boys.
He had his own CBS radio show from 1931. His soft crooning style used the microphone rather than projecting the voice, so it suited radio and records perfectly.

He hosted NBC's Kraft Music Hall from the mid-1930s to 1946 and recorded for Decca from 1934, becoming the best-selling recording artist of his time and making hundreds of records. Radio, records and film fed each other, a model of the modern entertainment industry.

He was a Paramount star, with the Road films with Bob Hope and Dorothy Lamour from Road to Singapore (1940). He won the Oscar for Best Actor as a priest in Going My Way (1944), awarded at the 1945 ceremony.

Irving Berlin's song White Christmas, sung by Crosby in Holiday Inn (1942), had a longing for home that made it the song of soldiers far from home. His recording is often called the best-selling single of all time.

Crosby entertained Allied troops through broadcasts for the forces, war-bond drives and a USO tour (the USO was the organisation that put on shows for American troops) of camps in England and France in 1944. His popularity with the forces was very high.

Contemporaries saw him as the most popular entertainer of the age, the relaxed, friendly face of America and an embodiment of easy-going American popular culture. His music spread the sounds of American radio into Europe.
Historians see him as central to the rise of recorded popular music and to American cultural influence in Europe, and they study his role in wartime morale alongside that of other entertainers.
notes.tip: Do not mix up Going My Way (his Oscar, 1944) with the Road films with Bob Hope. White Christmas (Crosby, Holiday Inn, 1942) is not We'll Meet Again (Vera Lynn, 1939) or Lili Marleen (Lale Andersen, German).

notes.h: The spread of American culture: jazz and reactions in Britain
notes.b: American popular culture crossed the Atlantic in the 1920s and 1930s, carried by records, radio and film. Europe's young embraced it, while their elders often worried.
points: The jazz age came to Europe with the Original Dixieland Jass Band in London (1919) and Josephine Baker in Paris (1925), and with dance crazes such as the Charleston.
American slang, clothes, hairstyles and film-star glamour were copied especially by the young.
British critics feared Americanisation, the spread of American habits and tastes, and worried about its effect on speech, taste and morals.
The film quota and the BBC's public-service ethos were partly defences against it. Audiences went on choosing American films and dance music anyway.
notes.tip: Name the forms of impact and argue them: leisure, news, politics, Americanisation of the young, reactions and wartime morale. Use named programmes, films, people and dates rather than general claims about the media.

notes.h: Reactions in the dictatorships
notes.b: The dictatorships treated American culture as a threat to their control and tried to ban it. The bans did not work as they hoped.
points: Nazi Germany banned jazz from German radio in 1935. In 1938 it showed jazz at the Degenerate Music exhibition in Düsseldorf as racially alien.
The Swing Youth (Swingjugend) of Hamburg and other cities defied the regime, for example by dancing to banned music, and faced arrest from 1941, with some sent to camps.
Fascist Italy promoted Italian films against Hollywood, for example through Cinecittà and the 1938 import monopoly.
Bans did not end American culture's appeal, because young people simply listened and danced in secret or in defiance.
notes.tip: Give named evidence: jazz banned from German radio in 1935, the 1938 Degenerate Music exhibition and the Swing Youth of Hamburg. Describe the Nazi attitude to jazz rather than putting a word in quotation marks as if it were a quotation.

notes.h: Wartime Americanisation
notes.b: The war put millions of Americans in Britain and put American music into British ears. This brought both admiration and resentment.
points: The first American troops arrived in Britain (in Northern Ireland) in January 1942, and there were well over a million by 1944. They brought swing music, chewing gum, nylons, cheap goods and money.
The reaction was admiration and resentment, summed up in the wartime British saying that they were "overpaid, oversexed and over here".

Vera Lynn, known as the Forces' Sweetheart, sang We'll Meet Again (1939), which became a symbol of separation and hope for servicemen and their families and was the British counterpart to White Christmas.
After 1945 American music and film dominated western Europe.

notes.h: Assessment: church-state relations under Mussolini and Hitler
notes.b: Judgements of church-state relations weigh the agreements and the Church's survival against the regimes' control of religious life. The best answers argue throughout who gained more.
points: Achievement for Mussolini: the Lateran Treaties ended the dispute with the papacy, brought Catholic support and prestige, and solved the Roman Question for the length of his regime.

Limit for Mussolini: the Church kept its own youth organisations, press and moral authority, and there were open disputes in 1931 and 1938. It was the one large organisation in Italy that stayed outside Fascist control, which set a limit on Italian totalitarianism.
Achievement for Hitler: the Concordat gave him prestige and ended the Centre Party and political Catholicism, and most churchgoers conformed.
Limit for Hitler: the Reichskirche failed to unify the Protestant churches. The Confessing Church and Galen showed that totalitarian control stopped at the church door.
Survival against failure: the churches survived both regimes as the largest institutions outside party control, but they did not defend the regimes' victims.
notes.tip: Higher Level judgement questions ask who gained more, the dictator or the Church, how far the churches resisted (defending their own rights or defending victims), and whether they show the limits of totalitarianism.

notes.h: Assessment: radio, cinema and popular culture
notes.b: Judgements of popular culture weigh its appeal against state control and cultural reaction. The same media could serve both freedom and propaganda.
points: Entertainment against persuasion: the same media served morale and propaganda, from BBC bulletins and Mrs Miniver to Lord Haw-Haw's broadcasts.
Democratic use against dictatorial control: BBC news, fireside chats and Chaplin's satire contrast with Nazi and Fascist bans and monopolies.
Americanisation as liberation for the young against a threat to national cultures: young people copied American music and film, while critics and dictators tried to restrict them.
Impact in war: radio and film lifted morale, and songs such as White Christmas, We'll Meet Again and Lili Marleen reached troops, while the BBC gave information to occupied Europe.
Chaplin's satire and Crosby's morale-building contrast with Riefenstahl, whose film work served the Nazi state as propaganda.
notes.tip: In personality essays, organise by theme (entertainment, politics, war), not three biographies. Show what Chaplin (comedy as art and satire of dictatorship) and Crosby (radio, records, film and troop morale) each contributed, and compare them.

notes.h: Assessment: contemporary and later views
notes.b: Views of these events changed with time. What contemporaries welcomed, later historians often questioned.
points: Contemporary view: the Lateran Treaties were welcomed by Catholics in 1929, including Catholics around the world.
Later view: critics say the Church lent Fascism respectability by signing, a bargain that made it complicit.
The Reich Concordat and Pius XII's wartime silence remain a continuing historians' debate.
Chaplin and Crosby were entertainers in their day, and they are now also historical evidence of the new mass culture.
Later historians stress that American popular culture spread widely in Europe in the 1930s and became a key influence on European youth, despite the dictatorships' attempts to restrict it.

keyTerms.definition: The Nazi plan for a single Protestant Reich Church under state control, pursued through the German Christians and the appointment of a Reich Bishop in 1933.
A formal agreement between the state and the papacy regulating the rights and status of the Catholic Church, as in the Italian Lateran Treaties of 1929 and the Reich Concordat of 1933.
The German Protestant movement formed in 1934 to oppose the state's control of the churches and the German Christians.
The organised spread of information and images to shape opinion and promote a regime, its leader and its policies.
The radio talks in which President Franklin Roosevelt addressed the American public directly from 1933.
The Hollywood system of the 1930s in which major studios controlled the production, distribution and cinemas that showed their films.
The agreements of 11 February 1929 that created Vatican City and settled the dispute between the Italian state and the papacy.
The 1931 encyclical of Pius XI protesting at the Fascist attack on Catholic Action.
The head of the planned Protestant Reich Church, a post given to Ludwig Müller in 1933.
The pro-Nazi movement in German Protestantism that backed a Reich Church and the exclusion of Jewish Christians.
Films with synchronised sound, which spread after The Jazz Singer in 1927.

factCards.term: Galen and the euthanasia programme: date
factCards.definition: Clemens August von Galen preached against the murder of people with disabilities in July and August 1941, and the programme was halted in August 1941.
The British Broadcasting Company was founded in 1922, and John Reith was its first director-general.
Franklin Roosevelt began his radio fireside chats in March 1933.

factCards.term: The Jazz Singer: year and significance
factCards.definition: Released in 1927, it introduced synchronised sound to mainstream cinema.

factCards.term: Cinematograph Films Act: year and purpose
factCards.definition: The 1927 Act required British cinemas to show a quota of British films.
